newsitem.title: UK: Brit Energy dips toe outside nuclear power.
newsitem.headline: Brit Energy dips toe outside nuclear power.

text.p: British Energy took its first steps outside nuclear power generation on Monday when it bought a 12.5 percent stake in a gas-fired power plant but analysts said it was little more than a toehold in the market.
"Although relatively modest, at least it's a step," said Nigel Hawkins of Yamaichi.
British Energy will take the stake in Humber Power Ltd, which owns and operates a 1,260 megawatt combined cycle gas power station at Stallingborough in northern England.
It will pay up to 20 million pounds ($33 million) and commit to subscribe for eight million pounds of short term loan stock, repayable in 2001.

"This investment is in line with British Energy's strategy to diversify its plant and fuel mix," the company said in a statement. Shares were up just half a penny by 1245 GMT to 134-1/2 pence, just off the session high of 135 pence.
Elf Exploration UK, a subsidiary of Elf Aquitaine, has also purchased a 12.5 percent interest in the plant on the same terms.
Other partners in the project are Finland's Imatran Voima Oy, Midlands Electricity, Japanese trading company Tomen Power Corporation and ABB Energy Ventures.
British Energy, privatised in June 1996, controls eight of the country's most modern nuclear power stations but wants to branch out into other forms of generation.
It looked at the possibility of building a gas generation plant at Heysham, northwest England, last year, but later abandoned the scheme.
Analysts said those plans had focused on an open cycle gas-fired station which is less efficient but also cheaper than Humber's combined cycle technology.
Humber's first phase of 750 megawatts is expected to be commissioned soon while the second phase of 510 megawatts should be onstream in 1999.

British Energy wants to diversify its capacity both to take advantage of competition in Britain, where the domestic electricity market should open up fully in 1998, and to enable expansion into international projects, analysts said.
"The company's core skill is nuclear generation and that is hard to exploit internationally because of antipathy towards nuclear power," said one analyst who asked not to be named.
"There are certainly compelling reasons to diversify beyond the eight nuclear stations," he said.
British Energy's current power station portfolio is particularly vulnerable to fluctuations in output demands and price on Britain's "pool" wholesale electricity market, analysts said.
The Humber deal could give British Energy some useful experience of generation outside nuclear, analysts said, but they were cautious over the longer-term benefits of this.
"British Energy does not appear to have an operational role, so it will gain some experience but it is not a big breakthrough for them," the analyst said.

"What does British Energy bring to the party other than its chequebook? If it wants the experience to set up its own consortium, the danger is it will still be seen as a weak contender and then have to overpay," the analyst said.
But another analyst who asked not to be identified felt British Energy would gain useful experience from the deal.
"It gives them a start and then we expect there will be other investments at home and abroad," this analyst said.
Hawkins said the deal was "sensible in the longer term but it's not going to be an overnight boom."
"They have to start somewhere and why not with Humber?" one analyst said.
($ = 0.611 British Pounds)
